source_text: CAPUT DECIMUM OCTAVUM, De attributis Dei tertii generis. Haec quoque de attributis secundi generis, quae Deo, ut viventi, respectu vitae intelligentis, conveniunt: sequuntur attributa tertii generis, quae illi tribuuntur respectu integritatis suae, affirmative notant summam perfectionem ejus, qua vivit integre. Haec attributa tertii generis continent eminentiam divinae ethicae, perinde ut attributa primi generis eminentiam divinae metaphysicae, et attributa secundi generis eminentiam divinae physicae declarant: et communiter exstant sub moralis integritatis seu perfectionis, rectitudinis, justitiae et sanctimoniae appellatione — Deut. XXXII.3-4; Matth. V.48; Lev. XI.44; I Pet. I.15.
english: CHAPTER EIGHTEEN. On Gods attributes of the third genus.

These things also concerning the attributes of the second genus, which belong to God as living with respect to intelligent life: there follow the attributes of the third genus, which are attributed to Him with respect to His integrity, and affirmatively note His highest perfection by which He lives integrally.

These attributes of the third genus contain the eminence of divine ethics, just as the attributes of the first genus declare the eminence of divine metaphysics, and those of the second genus the eminence of divine physics: and they commonly stand under the name of moral integrity or perfection, rectitude, justice, and holiness — Deuteronomy 32:3-4; Matthew 5:48; Leviticus 11:44; 1 Peter 1:15.

source_text: II. Sunt autem Dei virtus et beatitas. III. Virtus Dei est integritas intellectus ejus aut voluntatis. Virtus in Deo non est accidens, adeoque qualitas seu habitus intellectus et voluntatis, sed ipsissima Dei essentia considerata in ordine ad verum et bonum, et eminentia quaedam ejus quod in virtutibus et affectibus nostris perfectissimum est. Ipse enim sibi est ratio recta omnium scibilium et faciendorum. IV. Integritas intellectus est sapientia et prudentia. V. Sapientia est integritas intellectus, qua Deus novit quid cuique rei conveniat et quid ab ipsa sit alienum. Hac Deus intime novit se et res omnes, possibiles, futuras, existentes actu, praeteritas — Job XI; I Sam. II.3; Psal. CXXXIX; Rom. XI.33; I Tim. I.17; Heb. IV.13; I Joh. III.20. VI. Prudentia est integritas intellectus, qua Deus novit rebus omnibus in ordine ad praxin accommodare quod convenit. Hac Deus omnia decernit et facit ex sapientissimo consilio voluntatis suae — Isa. XL.28; Jer. X.12.
english: II. But Gods are virtue and blessedness. III. Gods virtue is the integrity of His intellect or will. Virtue in God is not an accident, and therefore not a quality or habit of intellect and will, but Gods very essence considered in order to the true and the good, and a certain eminence of that which in our virtues and affections is most perfect. For He Himself is to Himself the right reason of all things knowable and to be done.

IV. Integrity of intellect is wisdom and prudence. V. Wisdom is integrity of intellect by which God knows what agrees with each thing and what is alien from it. By this God most inwardly knows Himself and all things — possible, future, existing in act, past — Job 11; 1 Samuel 2:3; Psalm 139; Romans 11:33; 1 Timothy 1:17; Hebrews 4:13; 1 John 3:20.

VI. Prudence is integrity of intellect by which God knows how to accommodate to all things in order to practice what is fitting. By this God decrees and does all things from the most wise counsel of His will — Isaiah 40:28; Jeremiah 10:12.

source_text: VII. Integritas voluntatis est, quae in Deo concipitur per modum affectuum aut virtutum seu habituum moralium. VIII. Quae per modum affectuum concipitur, ea referri potest ad duo genera, quorum unum est eorum quos primos appellare possumus, alterum eorum qui a primis. IX. Primi affectus sunt unionis, ut amor; separationis, ut huic oppositum odium; aut communicationis, ut bonitas cum progressionibus suis, benignitate, gratia, misericordia. Amor est affectus unionis, quo Deus fertur in seipsum ut summe bonum, inque sui similia, ordinem bonumque justitiae, creaturam felicitatemque ejus. Amor Dei est activus aut passivus; activus duplex objectum habet, Deum ut bonum summum, et creaturas ut bonum inferius. Respectu Dei actus est mere naturalis ac necessarius; respectu creaturarum partim approbatio, partim favor seu benevolentia — Joh. III.16; Rom. V.8; I Joh. IV.8-10. XI. Ex dictis de amore Dei colligimus tres regulas: 1. Amor Dei quatenus est benevolentia erga creaturas prorsus est gratuitus et fons omnium bonorum. 2. Amor Dei certis gradibus juxta seriem rerum amabilium sapienter ordinatus est. 3. De speciali amore Dei quo nos in Christo complectitur, possumus certiores fieri ex ipsis divini amoris effectis. XII. Odium est affectus separationis, quo Deus injustitiam miseriamque creaturarum aversatur, creaturasque seipso et aliis minus amat. Primarium objectum est peccatum; odit et peccatores quatenus a pietatis studio alieni sunt — Psal. V.5; CXXXIX.21-22; Zach. VIII.17.
english: VII. Integrity of will is that which in God is conceived after the manner of affections or of virtues or moral habits. VIII. What is conceived after the manner of affections can be referred to two genera: those we can call primary, and those which arise from the primary. IX. Primary affections are of union, as love; of separation, as hatred opposite to this; or of communication, as goodness with its progressions — benignity, grace, mercy.

Love is the affection of union by which God is borne toward Himself as the highest good, and toward things like Himself, toward order and the good of justice, toward the creature and its happiness. Gods love is active or passive; the active has a double object — God as highest good, and creatures as a lesser good. With respect to God the act is merely natural and necessary; with respect to creatures partly approval, partly favor or benevolence — John 3:16; Romans 5:8; 1 John 4:8-10.

XI. From what has been said of Gods love we gather three rules: 1. Gods love as benevolence toward creatures is wholly gratuitous and the fountain of all goods. 2. Gods love is wisely ordered in certain degrees according to the series of lovable things. 3. Of Gods special love by which He embraces us in Christ we can be made more certain from the very effects of divine love. XII. Hatred is the affection of separation by which God turns from the injustice and misery of creatures, and loves creatures less than Himself and others. Its primary object is sin; He also hates sinners inasmuch as they are alien from the study of piety — Psalm 5:5; 139:21-22; Zechariah 8:17.

source_text: XIII. Bonitas est, qua Deus ad bonum extra se communicandum propendet. Bonum esse Deum praeter Scriptura omnia ipsius opera testantur — Psal. XXXIV.9; Matth. XIX.17; Luc. XVIII.19; Gen. I.31; contra Cerdonis, Marcionis et Manichaeorum haeresin. XIV. Benignitas est, qua Deus boni aliquid donando se creaturis suis beneficum exhibet. Primus divinae bonitatis progressus est benignitas; alia generalis erga omnes creaturas — Psal. CXLV.9; Matth. V.45; alia specialis erga electos. XV. Gratia est, qua Deus creaturis intelligentibus, nulla earum merita spectans, bonum aliquod impertit. Gratia excludit meritum creaturae; distinctiones gratiae in operantem et cooperantem, praevenientem, concomitantem et subsequentem, sufficientem et efficacem alibi expendimus. XVI. Misericordia Dei est affectus miseris, nihil obstante peccato, subveniendi. Misericordia Dei vel active accipitur vel passive; priore modo hic — Exod. XXXIV.6; Rom. IX.18; Eph. II.4; Tit. III.5. Sicut gratia est secundus bonitatis divinae progressus excludens meritum, ita misericordia est tertius illius progressus, remedium miseris inveniens.
english: XIII. Goodness is that by which God inclines toward communicating good outside Himself. That God is good, besides Scripture, all His works testify — Psalm 34:9; Matthew 19:17; Luke 18:19; Genesis 1:31; against the heresy of Cerdo, Marcion, and the Manichees.

XIV. Benignity is that by which God, by giving some good, shows Himself beneficent to His creatures. The first progression of divine goodness is benignity; one general toward all creatures — Psalm 145:9; Matthew 5:45; another special toward the elect. XV. Grace is that by which God imparts some good to intelligent creatures, regarding none of their merits. Grace excludes the creatures merit; distinctions of grace into operating and cooperating, prevenient, concomitant and subsequent, sufficient and efficacious, we treat elsewhere.

XVI. Gods mercy is the affection of coming to the aid of the miserable, nothing obstructing by reason of sin. Gods mercy is taken actively or passively; here in the former way — Exodus 34:6; Romans 9:18; Ephesians 2:4; Titus 3:5. Just as grace is the second progression of divine goodness excluding merit, so mercy is its third progression, finding a remedy for the miserable.

source_text: XVII. Atque haec de attributis Dei quae analogiam habent cum affectibus quasi primis: sequuntur attributa quae analoga sunt affectibus quasi ortis a primis, qui non circa bonum et malum communiter, sed in specie circa illud qua praesens aut absens est occupantur, et distinguuntur e nostra considerationis modo, quatenus vel in concupiscibili vel in irascibili concipiuntur. XVIII. In concupiscibili primo est desiderium et abominatio, deinde gaudium et dolor. XIX. Desiderium est quasi affectus Dei res naturae suae convenientes, fidem et opera pietatis atque justitiae creaturis intelligentibus a se praescripta et per gratiam suam praestabilia, obtinendi. XX. Abominatio est, qua Deus res a natura sua abhorrentes, infidelitatem, opera impietatis et iniquitatis, omissionemque remunerationis, exsecratur. XXI. Gaudium est, quo Deus in re bona tanquam praesente et sibi voluntatique suae congruente delectatur. XXII. Dolor est, quo Deus se habet ad sensum mali praesentis. XXV. Spes est, qua Deus bonum opimum prosequitur. XXVII. Confidentia est, qua Deus ingenti spiritu bonum desideratum persequitur. XXVIII. Metus est, quo Deus malum, ut futurum possibile, declinat. XXIX. Ira est affectus depulsionis, quo Deus creaturam peccantem punire vult — Psal.; Deut.; Ezech.
english: XVII. And these things concerning Gods attributes which have analogy with affections as it were primary: there follow attributes analogous to affections as it were arising from the primary, which are occupied not about good and evil commonly, but in species about that as present or absent, and are distinguished from the mode of our consideration inasmuch as they are conceived either in the concupiscible or in the irascible.

XVIII. In the concupiscible first is desire and abomination, then joy and grief. XIX. Desire is as it were Gods affection of obtaining things agreeing with His nature — faith and works of piety and justice prescribed by Himself to intelligent creatures and performable through His grace. XX. Abomination is that by which God execrates things abhorrent from His nature — unbelief, works of impiety and iniquity, and omission of remuneration.

XXI. Joy is that by which God delights in a good thing as present and agreeing with Himself and His will. XXII. Grief is that by which God holds Himself toward the sense of present evil. XXV. Hope is that by which God pursues the best good. XXVII. Confidence is that by which God with great spirit pursues the desired good. XXVIII. Fear is that by which God declines evil as a possible future. XXIX. Wrath is the affection of driving away by which God wills to punish the sinning creature.

source_text: XXX. Haec sunt attributa Dei quae analogiam habent cum affectibus: sequuntur ea quae analoga sunt virtutibus moralibus, tanquam affectuum istorum moderatricibus, respiciunt vel ad omnes affectus generaliter, ut justitia, vel ad aliquos dumtaxat, ut patientia quae iram et poenas ex ira moderantur. XXXI. Justitia est, qua Dei voluntas constans est ad suum sibi et alii cuique tribuendum. Est quidem justitia Dei per se et reipsa unica, sicut unica ejus essentia est. XXXII. Universalis est, qua Deus actiones suas infinitae naturae suae rectitudini convenienter dirigit. XXXIII. Particularis est, qua Deus, prout status personae quam in certa aliqua actione sua respicit, suum cuique tribuit. XXXIV. Estque primo erga se aut erga creaturas. XXXV. Erga se est, qua Deus sibi ipsi tribuit et ab aliis tribui vult eam gloriam quae ipsi ut summo bono debetur. XXXVI. Erga creaturas est, qua Deus nulli creaturae, quicquid de ea statuat aut faciat, iniuriam infert. XXXVIII. Disponens est, qua Deus omnia sapientissime ordinat.
english: XXX. These are Gods attributes which have analogy with affections: there follow those which are analogous to moral virtues, as moderators of those affections; they look either to all affections generally, as justice, or to some only, as patience which moderates wrath and punishments from wrath.

XXXI. Justice is that by which Gods will is constant toward rendering to Himself and to each other what is his. Gods justice is indeed through itself and in the thing itself one, just as His essence is one. XXXII. Universal is that by which God directs His actions conveniently to the rectitude of His infinite nature. XXXIII. Particular is that by which God, according to the status of the person which He regards in some certain action of His, renders to each his own.

XXXIV. And it is first toward Himself or toward creatures. XXXV. Toward Himself is that by which God renders to Himself and wills to be rendered by others that glory which is owed to Him as highest good. XXXVI. Toward creatures is that by which God does injury to no creature, whatever He decrees or does concerning it. XXXVIII. Disposing is that by which God most wisely orders all things.

source_text: Justitia irae est, qua Deus judicia sua quae comminatus est aequissime exercet. Justitia vindicans est, qua Deus reprobos perdit; hanc Deus exercet tum in reprobis hujus vitae, tum in aeterna damnatione. Justitia facti est, qua Deus quicquid decernendo aut exsequendo facit, rectitudini suae infinitae convenienter facit. Patientia est, qua Deus iram et poenas moderatur. LI. Longanimitas est, qua Deus iram, ne properet ad depulsionem mali quam primum id creatura meretur, suspendit — Psal. CIII.8-9; Nah. I.3. LII. Mansuetudo est, qua Deus iram suam temperat, ne nimia sit, ac ne gravitas illius scelerum magnitudini respondeat — Psal. XXX.6; CIII.10-11; Jerem. III.12. LIV. Clementia est, qua Deus debitas poenas ita moderatur, ut vires creaturae haud superent, et meritis peccatorum gravitate et diuturnitate sint multo inferiores — II Sam. VII.14-15; Psal. LXXXIX.33-34; Joel II.13; Exod. XXII.27. Ex his de attributis Dei tertii generis probe constitutis, sequitur CAPUT DECIMUM NONUM, De Dei beatitudine.
english: Justice of wrath is that by which God most equitably exercises His judgments which He has threatened. Vindicating justice is that by which God destroys the reprobate; this God exercises both in the reprobate of this life and in eternal damnation. Justice of deed is that by which God, whatever He does in decreeing or executing, does conveniently to His infinite rectitude.

Patience is that by which God moderates wrath and punishments. LI. Longsuffering is that by which God suspends wrath, lest He hasten to drive away evil as soon as the creature merits it — Psalm 103:8-9; Nahum 1:3. LII. Meekness is that by which God tempers His wrath, lest it be too great, and lest its severity answer to the magnitude of crimes — Psalm 30:6; 103:10-11; Jeremiah 3:12.

LIV. Clemency is that by which God so moderates due punishments that they by no means surpass the creatures strength, and are much inferior to the merits of sins in gravity and duration — 2 Samuel 7:14-15; Psalm 89:33-34; Joel 2:13; Exodus 22:27. From these things rightly established concerning Gods attributes of the third genus, there follows CHAPTER NINETEEN, On Gods blessedness.
